question.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(\pi ,0)?$
question.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\pi ,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+2xy)\text{ }i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+{x}^{2})\text{ }j \\ -∇f(\pi ,0) & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡0+2\cdot \pi \cdot 0)\text{ }i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡0+{\pi }^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =i-{\pi }^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $i-{\pi }^{2}\,j.$
